title: Faith as the True Seal and Inheritance Beyond Law
english: When the faithful turn aside like the sealed, the mystery of those justified by faith unfolds. Those who, after believing, emerge from Abraham’s circumcision—yet remain distinct from the faithful—may be counted as his children or reckoned as his offspring, forming a people apart from the uncircumcised justified by faith. The seal remained intact as long as no one from faith and uncircumcision had arrived. But when the foretold people formed from the uncircumcised justified by faith appeared, the seal and its sign were loosed, so that it could be said to the one desiring that seal: if you circumcise, Christ profits you nothing. For the law brings wrath; where there is no law, there is no transgression. Therefore, the promise comes through faith, so that it may rest upon grace, ensuring the promise is sure for all Abraham’s seed—not only those under the law, but also those who share Abraham’s faith, who is father of us all, as it is written: ‘I have made you a father of many nations.’ Before him, he believed in God, who gives life to the dead and calls into being what does not exist. One must hear the apostle here without contention and grasp his intent. Some claim: ‘If there is no law nor transgression in that place, then surely no one transgressed before Moses.’ But if no one transgressed, then no one is blameworthy—not Cain, nor those who perished in the flood due to their own sins, nor the Sodomites in transgression, nor even Adam and Eve. Yet it must be told them: the Mosaic law does not work wrath in judgment, but wrath according to itself—making some stonecutters, others burning in fire, or subjecting others to another punishment. Even where there is no law nor transgression, the law still speaks to those under the law. Observe them and the law beside Paul, called the law of faith, which works God’s wrath, and where transgression occurs when the law of faith and the law of God intersect. But clearly, he is another law—namely, the law of God, by which alone he delights in the inward man. Yet another law exists: the law in his members, warring against the law of the mind. Beware lest this be the true worker of wrath; and where there is no law, this is neither transgression. Those under this law are in no way heirs, for if those under the law are heirs, faith is rendered void. In the catalogue of charismata distributed according to the measure of faith, faith itself is enumerated—for Paul says, with other gifts, to another faith in the same Spirit. And elsewhere he declares that from God he has graciously granted you not only to attain Christ, but also to suffer for his sake. But I think the apostles, being weakly persuaded, are to be in the faith that dwells in us… Even if the heirs and the promise are to be according to grace, yet this faith which precedes grace—by which it is said that it is of faith that it might be according to grace—cannot subsist without grace. And to all the seed, he says: either to those of the law or to those of Abraham’s faith, and not only to those of the law, but also if one should possess Abraham’s faith in addition to the law. For if we do not thus obtain, the promise will fall to those from Ishmael and those from Keturah, which is not pleasing. (Of the same) It is necessary, he says, it appears, to examine how being according to faith and according to grace follows the promise being sure; for if it were of the law, obtaining the sure promise would be impossible. Therefore, consider, as if a dyer were dyeing: the dyeing is made by faith concerning the soul, and especially the reasoning accounted to righteousness, so that the promise and grace through it might possess, by its inexhaustibility or immutability, certainty—which does not appear concerning the works of the law. Sometimes he feeds the righteous from his own righteousness and does evil; but I do not know whether it is written concerning faith that anyone has turned away from faith, having once been testified to have believed and been justified by faith. Then also the divine apostle seals with his testimony the thing said to him. (Of the same) [But what he says this is: as God is not a partial God but the Father of all, so also he; and again, as God is Father not according to natural kinship but according to the familiarity of faith, so also he; for obedience makes a father of all of us. Since neither]

title: Faith's Paradox: God's Power in Human Weakness
english: They regarded their kinship as having grasped the stronger one, thus exhibiting lordship over the word of God and lifting it upward. Following this, he demonstrates that he received this as a reward of faith; therefore, if this were not true, even if he were father of all who dwell on earth, the opposite would have no room—since the opposite is identical in nature. This is the paradox: those he did not possess by nature, he received as God’s gift. Such, he says, were the many nations whom the God who gives promises to him appointed as father. Regarding those made dead through sin, whose soul has become dead within a living body, I now believe he says: the sinner’s own soul will die. But what of those who are not, or those deprived of being and not sharing in it—thus called in opposition to those who partake in the one who said, ‘I am he who is’? He calls those who are not, so that, by obeying them, he may grant them the gift of being. Yet perhaps someone will object: how does the apostle elsewhere say that God chose the non-existent things in order to abolish the existing things? But it is clear this is a different sense of ‘existing’ and ‘non-existing,’ apart from every composition there: those existing here are the strong, the powerful, the well-born; those not existing are those otherwise disposed in relation to these, as regards their opinion. [[Romans 4:18–22 >> Bible:Romans 4:18-22]] He who against hope believed in hope, that he might become father of many nations according to what was said, so will your offspring be; and not having weakened in faith, he considered his own body already dead, being about a hundred years old, and the deadening of Sarah’s womb; but in regard to God’s promise, he was not weakened by unbelief but was strengthened by faith, giving glory to God and being fully convinced that what he promised is able and to do; therefore it was credited to him for righteousness. See lest perhaps as Abraham believed against hope, from hope to hope, so also all who are sons of Abraham by faith believe against hope, from hope to hope, concerning all things, whether concerning the resurrection of the dead or concerning inheriting the heavenly kingdom or the kingdom of God. For these things, insofar as they are upon human nature, are against hope; but insofar as they are upon the power of God and his truthful promises, upon hope those who from faith hope attain. And since the one who believes upon hope believes, therefore he remains in faith, hope; from which these are born, and the third greater than these is love; and I suppose that faith has the logic of elementary instruction, hope of progress, love of perfection. But that it is said that Abraham’s body is deadened not because of old age will be evident to the one who has considered how Abraham, having set forth, took a wife named Keturah; and he bore her after Sarah’s death, who lived one hundred twenty-seven years; and Abraham is clearly found to be ten years older than Sarah. If therefore, as some say, through the promise he caused Isaac to be educated, how then, apart from promise, after one hundred twenty years did he bear those from Keturah? Therefore it is said in praise that such a deadening of the members upon the earth mortifies; for when someone by spirit does the deeds of the body to death, then he extinguishes all the innate fire to burn within him; therefore that Isaac’s birth is not from burning but from God’s promise; for they have become worthy to be called parents of this patriarch. [[Romans 4:23–25 >> Bible:Romans 4:23-25]] It was not written only because of him that he was credited, but also because of us to whom it is going to be credited who believe in the one who raised our Lord Jesus from the dead, who was delivered because of our transgressions and was raised because of our justification. Now the ‘because of him alone’ has been taken instead of ‘concerning him alone’; but also the ‘because of us’ instead of ‘concerning us’; for not in order that Abraham, having met Moses the earlier writer, might be benefited by the later letter of him. But if it is not written only concerning Abraham that he was credited to righteousness, but also concerning us, as if the Word were proclaiming beforehand the righteousness to be credited from faith to those who believe in the one who raised Jesus Christ from the dead, then take heed lest perhaps only and every believer upon the one who raised our Lord Jesus from the dead, the one raised with Christ, might say and also rise and dwell in us in the heavenly places in Christ; having been raised together with Christ, the one having become conformed to his resurrection, and because of having died together with him, lives with him; for if we die and live, he died with Christ, since Christ, having died.

He regarded their kinship as having seized the stronger one, thereby displaying lordship over the word of God and lifting it upward. After these things, he also shows that he received this as a recompense of faith; therefore, if this is not the case, even if he is father of all who inhabit the earth, the opposite no longer has space; for the opposite is the same. For this is the paradox: those whom he did not have by nature, he received these from God's gift. Such, he says, were the many nations whom the God who gives the promises to him appointed as father. Concerning those who through sin have been made dead, whose soul has become dead in a living body, I now suppose he says: the soul of the sinner itself will die. title: The Once-for-All Death to Sin and Life in Christ
english: He endured death to sin in a single, definitive act; and he, having died to sin, now lives in communion with Christ. Indeed, the one who walks in newness of life walks with Christ. For the love of God has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit, who was given to us. This occurred precisely when we were still powerless: Christ died at the appointed moment for the ungodly. It is rare for someone to lay down their life for a righteous person—perhaps only for a genuinely good person might one find the courage to die. Yet God reveals his own love toward us in that, while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. Consequently, since we have now been justified by his blood, we shall be saved through him from the wrath of God. When the text speaks of the weak or sinners, it names them and draws them into communion; but when it refers to the ungodly, it does not name them. Perhaps this distinction reflects the condition of those who live under the law: they strive by their own strength, and thus remain weak and sinful, yet they are not labeled 'ungodly' in the ordinary scriptural sense—because those under the law who transgress against God are called sinners, not ungodly. The truly ungodly are those who, though they claim to live under the law and possess its knowledge, have abandoned the God of their ancestors and turned to the gods of the nations. Before we turned to God in reverence, love had not taken root within us, for we all loved something more than God. But in that very condition—while we were still such—Christ died for us, and only then was the love of God established and made firm within us, after every obstacle to its presence had been removed by the death of Jesus. From this we must therefore listen to the ongoing establishment and confirmation of God’s love within us, a love that belongs properly to none other than God himself. As we do not merely await immortal life, but even now, as those who have become acquainted with God, are exalted in our contemplation of the Lord Christ—who, having become our mediator, brought about peace—we are called to this awareness. Therefore, if we have truly been united with him in the likeness of his death, we shall most certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection. He planted a name, having come to know a certain plant—namely, the death of Jesus—which bears fruit that destroys sin. To this plant, the word tills among those who have received instruction through Christ, making them one with him in the likeness of his death. While human nature can assume a certain likeness of that death, it cannot take on his actual death, lest it fall into sin or even come to know sin. But having died—not to cleanse sin in himself, but to cleanse sin in us—no one who has sinned can die in that same way. For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, yet are justified freely, and the rest follows. In other passages, he says: God raised him up and seated him with himself in the heavenly realms in Christ; and if you have been raised with Christ, seek the things above. How, then, does he say here that we too shall be in the resurrection? Let it be understood that the apostle speaks of the resurrection in two ways: first, the resurrection in which the holy one has already risen with Christ and, having risen with him, now seeks the things above; second, the resurrection that will occur when the perfect comes—of which Daniel the prophet prophesied, saying that many who sleep in the dust of the earth shall awake, some to everlasting life, and some to shame and everlasting contempt. Thus, the saints affirm concerning the first resurrection that they have already risen with Christ; but concerning the second, they declare that they shall rise again. If we have died with Christ, we believe we shall also live with him, knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death no longer holds dominion over him. For what he died to, he died to sin once for all; and what he lives for, he lives to God. So too, you should regard yourselves as truly dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord. He boldly affirms that death no longer rules over him—an idea that seems disgraceful to many, who claim he did not die to escape death’s rule, but willingly surrendered his soul for his sheep, or for his friends. For the Savior himself declares: No one takes my life from me; I lay it down of my own accord. Then someone might object, saying that death is now called the middle and indifferent state, as the common saying goes, that he died at that time, just as Paul says he died according to the Scriptures. But how can this be reconciled with the narrative that we died with Christ, and that what he died for, he died to sin once for all?
